brief.summary: A dotfiles manager for hobbyist tinkerers that keeps one person's shell, editor, git and terminal settings in sync across all their machines, with per-machine overrides.
brief.user: Tomasz, a hospital pharmacist who writes Python and tinkers with home servers on evenings and weekends. He knows his way around zsh and Neovim but doesn't want to hand-edit symlinks and if-statements in his configs anymore.
brief.moment: He's just added a new Raspberry Pi 5 that will run his home media server, and he's deciding which of his settings it should inherit. His prompt currently shows git status and the battery level, which make no sense on a headless Pi and slow down logins over SSH. He wants the Pi to get his aliases and git identity but a stripped-down prompt, no Neovim plugins that need Node, and a different default editor font size for when he occasionally plugs in a monitor. brief.data: Three machines: 'thinkpad-x1' (Arch Linux, primary, last synced 2 hours ago), 'mac-mini-studio' (macOS 15, last synced 9 days ago, 3 local changes not yet pushed), and the new 'pi-media' (Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm, never synced). 41 tracked config files including .zshrc (312 lines), starship.toml, init.lua plus 27 plugin specs, .gitconfig, tmux.conf, alacritty.toml and ssh config. 64 shell aliases grouped by origin (git, docker, pacman, homebrew). Prompt segments: directory, git branch, git dirty count, python venv, battery, command duration, clock. Settings with values per machine, e.g. editor font size 13 on thinkpad and 15 on mac-mini; git signing key set on thinkpad only. Two conflicts: alias 'up' means pacman update on Arch and brew upgrade on macOS; the PATH line for ~/.cargo/bin is duplicated on mac-mini.

prompt:
I need the front end for Dotwell. A dotfiles manager for hobbyist tinkerers that keeps one person's shell, editor, git and terminal settings in sync across all their machines, with per-machine overrides.

Who's using it: Tomasz, a hospital pharmacist who writes Python and tinkers with home servers on evenings and weekends. He knows his way around zsh and Neovim but doesn't want to hand-edit symlinks and if-statements in his configs anymore.

What they're doing right now: He's just added a new Raspberry Pi 5 that will run his home media server, and he's deciding which of his settings it should inherit. His prompt currently shows git status and the battery level, which make no sense on a headless Pi and slow down logins over SSH. He wants the Pi to get his aliases and git identity but a stripped-down prompt, no Neovim plugins that need Node, and a different default editor font size for when he occasionally plugs in a monitor. Before he applies anything, he wants to see exactly what the Pi will end up with compared to his laptop, and he doesn't want to accidentally change the laptop.

What's in the system at this point: Three machines: 'thinkpad-x1' (Arch Linux, primary, last synced 2 hours ago), 'mac-mini-studio' (macOS 15, last synced 9 days ago, 3 local changes not yet pushed), and the new 'pi-media' (Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm, never synced). 41 tracked config files including .zshrc (312 lines), starship.toml, init.lua plus 27 plugin specs, .gitconfig, tmux.conf, alacritty.toml and ssh config. 64 shell aliases grouped by origin (git, docker, pacman, homebrew). Prompt segments: directory, git branch, git dirty count, python venv, battery, command duration, clock. Settings with values per machine, e.g. editor font size 13 on thinkpad and 15 on mac-mini; git signing key set on thinkpad only. Two conflicts: alias 'up' means pacman update on Arch and brew upgrade on macOS; the PATH line for ~/.cargo/bin is duplicated on mac-mini.

Build it as a working web app, opened in the state that person would see at that moment. No backend: use realistic mock data (no lorem ipsum, no placeholder names), and make the interactive parts actually work client-side.

Use whatever framework and tooling you like. When you're done there must be a static production build in ./out with ./out/index.html as the entry point. It will be served from the root of a plain static file server (no rewrites, no server code) and viewed in a desktop browser at 1440×900.
